about: Analysis 1 (MATH40002) is a core 10-ECTS module in Year 1 of Imperial's Mathematics BSc. The 2026-27 departmental handbook lists it as running from week 5 of Term 1 through Term 2, with about 40 lectures and 14 classes, and says core modules must be passed (after resits if necessary) to progress to Year 2. The handbook describes it as a rigorous treatment of limits of real and complex numbers: limits of sequences and series, continuity and differentiability, and the limiting constructions behind the integral of a function of one variable. It gives no detailed topic list, so the eight topics here are a standard first analysis course built from that description. Summative assessment in 2026-27 is 10% for a 1-hour exam in week 1 of Term 2, 10% for a 1-hour in-class test in week 6 of Term 2, 10% for assessed problems, and 70% for a 2-hour final exam in Term 3.
topics: The real numbers: completeness and suprema
Limits of real and complex sequences
Monotone sequences, subsequences and Cauchy sequences
Differentiability and the mean value theorem
The Riemann integral and the fundamental theorem of calculus

notes.h: Completeness, suprema and the Archimedean property
notes.body:
Analysis begins by saying precisely what the real numbers are. ℝ is an ordered field, like ℚ, but it has one extra property, completeness. Almost every major theorem in the course (monotone convergence, Bolzano–Weierstrass, the intermediate value theorem, the existence of integrals) ultimately depends on it. In this pack ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}.

Bounds
- A set A ⊆ ℝ is bounded above if there is M with a ≤ M for all a ∈ A. Such an M is an upper bound. Lower bounds are defined in the same way.
- s is the supremum (least upper bound) of A, written s = sup A, if (i) s is an upper bound of A and (ii) every upper bound M of A satisfies s ≤ M.
- Equivalent working form: s = sup A if and only if s is an upper bound and, for every ε > 0, there is a ∈ A with a > s − ε.
- The supremum need not belong to A. If it does, it is the maximum of A. The infimum (greatest lower bound) is defined in the same way.

The completeness axiom
- Every non-empty subset of ℝ that is bounded above has a supremum in ℝ.
- Both hypotheses matter. The empty set is bounded above by every real number but has no least upper bound. ℕ is non-empty but not bounded above.
- ℚ is not complete. The set {q ∈ ℚ : q² < 2} is non-empty and bounded above, but has no supremum in ℚ, because its supremum in ℝ is √2, which is irrational.
- By applying the axiom to −A, every non-empty subset of ℝ that is bounded below has an infimum.

Consequences
- Archimedean property: ℕ is not bounded above in ℝ. So for every ε > 0 there is n ∈ ℕ with 1/n < ε.
- Proof sketch: if ℕ were bounded above, s = sup ℕ would exist. Then s − 1 is not an upper bound, so some n > s − 1, which gives n + 1 > s, a contradiction.
- Density: between any two distinct reals there is a rational (and an irrational).
- Existence of roots: for example, there is a unique x > 0 with x² = 2, namely sup{x > 0 : x² < 2}.

Worked example: A = {1 − 1/n : n ∈ ℕ}.
- Every element is less than 1, so 1 is an upper bound.
- Given ε > 0, the Archimedean property gives n with 1/n < ε, and then 1 − 1/n > 1 − ε. So sup A = 1.
- 1 is not in A, so A has no maximum.
- The smallest element is 0 (at n = 1), so inf A = min A = 0.

Inequalities you will use constantly
- The triangle inequality: |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y|.
- The reverse triangle inequality: ||x| − |y|| ≤ |x − y|.
- Both hold for complex numbers with |z| the modulus. ℂ cannot be ordered, so sup and inf make sense only for real sets.

Exam tips: when asked to find a supremum, prove both parts. Show it is an upper bound, then use the ε form (often with the Archimedean property) to show nothing smaller works. Always check whether the supremum is attained.

notes.h: Convergence of sequences: definition and limit laws
notes.body:
A sequence is a function from ℕ to ℝ (or ℂ), written (a_n). The definition of a limit is the single most important definition in the course. You need to be able to state it exactly and use it in proofs.

Definition
- (a_n) converges to a, written a_n → a, if for every ε > 0 there exists N ∈ ℕ such that |a_n − a| < ε for all n ≥ N.
- The order of the quantifiers matters: N may depend on ε, but it must work for every n ≥ N.
- A sequence that does not converge diverges. a_n → ∞ means: for every M there is N with a_n > M for all n ≥ N. This is a kind of divergence, not convergence to a number.
- Complex sequences use the same definition with |·| as the modulus. z_n → z if and only if Re z_n → Re z and Im z_n → Im z.

How to write an ε–N proof
- Example: prove that (2n + 1)/(n + 3) → 2.
- Rough work: |(2n + 1)/(n + 3) − 2| = 5/(n + 3) < 5/n.
- Proof: given ε > 0, choose N ∈ ℕ with N > 5/ε (possible by the Archimedean property). Then for n ≥ N, |a_n − 2| < 5/n ≤ 5/N < ε.
- Do the algebra first, then write the proof in the right logical order.

Basic theorems
- Limits are unique.
- A convergent sequence is bounded. (Take ε = 1. Then |a_n| < |a| + 1 for n ≥ N, and only finitely many terms come before N.) The converse is false: (−1)ⁿ is bounded but diverges.
- Algebra of limits: if a_n → a and b_n → b, then a_n + b_n → a + b, a_nb_n → ab, λa_n → λa, and a_n/b_n → a/b provided b ≠ 0. (b_n is then non-zero for all large n.)
- Sandwich (squeeze) theorem: if a_n ≤ c_n ≤ b_n for all large n, and a_n → L and b_n → L, then c_n → L.
- Limits preserve weak inequalities: if a_n ≤ b_n for all n, then lim a_n ≤ lim b_n. Strict inequalities can become equalities, for example 0 < 1/n but the limit is 0.

Standard limits
- 1/n^p → 0 for p > 0.
- zⁿ → 0 if |z| < 1, and (zⁿ) diverges if |z| > 1. For |z| = 1 it converges only when z = 1.
- n^(1/n) → 1.
- For any fixed x, xⁿ/n! → 0.
- For |x| < 1, n^k xⁿ → 0 for any fixed k: polynomial growth loses to geometric decay.

Worked example: (3n² − n)/(n² + 5) = (3 − 1/n)/(1 + 5/n²) → 3/1 = 3, by the algebra of limits. Dividing top and bottom by the highest power of n is the standard technique.

Worked example: (−1)ⁿ/n → 0, because |(−1)ⁿ/n| = 1/n → 0. In general, |a_n| → 0 implies a_n → 0.

Exam tips: state the definition before using it, choose N explicitly in terms of ε, and when you apply the algebra of limits, check that each part converges and that you are not dividing by a limit of zero.

notes.h: Monotone convergence, Bolzano–Weierstrass and Cauchy sequences
notes.body:
Often we need to show that a sequence converges without knowing its limit in advance. The three tools in this topic do that, and all of them rely on completeness.

Monotone convergence theorem
- If (a_n) is increasing (a_n ≤ a_{n+1} for all n) and bounded above, then it converges, and its limit is sup{a_n : n ∈ ℕ}.
- Likewise, a decreasing sequence that is bounded below converges to its infimum.
- Proof idea: let s = sup{a_n}. Given ε > 0, some a_N > s − ε. Since the sequence is increasing, s − ε < a_N ≤ a_n ≤ s for all n ≥ N.

Worked example: a_1 = 1 and a_{n+1} = √(2 + a_n).
- Induction gives 0 < a_n < 2 and a_n < a_{n+1}. (If a_n < 2 then a_{n+1} = √(2 + a_n) < √4 = 2. Also a_{n+1}² − a_n² = 2 + a_n − a_n² = (2 − a_n)(1 + a_n) > 0.)
- So the sequence converges to some L. Letting n → ∞ in the recurrence gives L = √(2 + L), so L² − L − 2 = 0 and L = 2 or L = −1.
- Since every a_n > 0, L ≥ 0, so L = 2.
- Note: you must prove convergence before solving for L. The equation alone does not show the limit exists.

Another example: (1 + 1/n)ⁿ is increasing and bounded above (by 3, using the binomial theorem), so it converges. Its limit is e.

Subsequences
- A subsequence is (a_{n_k}) with n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < …. If a_n → a, then every subsequence also tends to a.
- So if two subsequences have different limits, the sequence diverges. This is the standard way to show (−1)ⁿ diverges.
- Every real sequence has a monotone subsequence. One proof uses 'peak' indices: n is a peak if a_n ≥ a_m for all m > n.

Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem
- Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence.
- The same holds in ℂ: apply the theorem to the real parts, then to the imaginary parts of that subsequence.
- Proof: take a monotone subsequence. It is bounded, so it converges by the monotone convergence theorem.
- Boundedness is essential. The sequence a_n = n has no convergent subsequence.

Cauchy sequences
- (a_n) is Cauchy if for every ε > 0 there exists N such that |a_m − a_n| < ε for all m, n ≥ N.
- Every convergent sequence is Cauchy, by the triangle inequality with ε/2.
- In ℝ and ℂ, every Cauchy sequence converges (the general principle of convergence). Proof: a Cauchy sequence is bounded, so by Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a convergent subsequence. A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit.
- The Cauchy criterion lets you prove convergence without knowing the limit. It fails in ℚ: decimal approximations to √2 form a Cauchy sequence of rationals with no rational limit.
- Warning: |a_{n+1} − a_n| → 0 does not make a sequence Cauchy. The partial sums of the harmonic series, and √n, are counterexamples.

Upper and lower limits (if covered)
- limsup a_n is the largest limit of a subsequence, and liminf a_n the smallest. A bounded sequence converges if and only if they are equal.

Exam tips: for recursive sequences, prove boundedness and monotonicity by induction, then find the limit and use the bounds to rule out the wrong root. Quote theorems with their full hypotheses, such as 'bounded and monotone' or 'bounded sequence of reals'.

notes.h: Infinite series: convergence and comparison tests
notes.body:
An infinite series Σa_n is defined through its sequence of partial sums, s_N = a_1 + … + a_N. The series converges to S if s_N → S. Everything about series is really about sequences, so all of the previous topic applies.

First facts
- If Σa_n converges, then a_n → 0. (a_n = s_n − s_{n−1}, and both partial sums tend to S.)
- The converse is false, and this is the most common error in the topic. a_n → 0 does not imply that Σa_n converges.
- Convergent series can be added and multiplied by constants term by term. Changing finitely many terms does not affect whether a series converges (although it can change the sum).
- Cauchy criterion for series: Σa_n converges if and only if for every ε > 0 there is N with |a_{n+1} + … + a_m| < ε for all m > n ≥ N.

Geometric series
- Σ_{n=0}^∞ zⁿ = 1/(1 − z) for |z| < 1, and the series diverges for |z| ≥ 1 (the terms do not tend to 0).
- Watch the starting index: Σ_{n=1}^∞ zⁿ = z/(1 − z).

The harmonic series and p-series
- Σ1/n diverges, even though 1/n → 0. Group the terms: 1 + 1/2 + (1/3 + 1/4) + (1/5 + … + 1/8) + …. Each bracket is at least 1/2, so s_{2^k} ≥ 1 + k/2.
- Σ1/n^p converges if and only if p > 1.

Series of non-negative terms
- If a_n ≥ 0, the partial sums increase. So Σa_n converges if and only if the partial sums are bounded (monotone convergence).
- Comparison test: if 0 ≤ a_n ≤ b_n for all large n and Σb_n converges, then Σa_n converges. If Σa_n diverges, then Σb_n diverges.
- Limit comparison test: if a_n, b_n > 0 and a_n/b_n → L with 0 < L < ∞, then Σa_n and Σb_n either both converge or both diverge.
- Cauchy condensation test: if (a_n) is non-negative and decreasing, then Σa_n converges if and only if Σ2^k a_{2^k} converges. Applied to 1/n^p, it gives the geometric series Σ(2^{1−p})^k, which converges if and only if p > 1.

Worked example: Σ1/n² converges.
- For n ≥ 2, 1/n² < 1/(n(n − 1)) = 1/(n − 1) − 1/n.
- The right-hand side telescopes, so Σ_{n=2}^N 1/(n(n − 1)) = 1 − 1/N < 1.
- So the partial sums of Σ1/n² are bounded by 2, and the series converges.

Alternating series test (Leibniz)
- If (a_n) is decreasing and a_n → 0 (so a_n ≥ 0), then Σ(−1)^{n+1}a_n converges.
- The error after N terms is at most a_{N+1}.
- Example: 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + … converges (its sum is ln 2), even though Σ1/n diverges.
- Both conditions are needed. Decreasing alone is not enough unless a_n → 0, and a_n → 0 alone is not enough without monotonicity.

Exam tips: always check a_n → 0 first; if it fails, the series diverges and you are done. For positive terms, compare with a p-series or a geometric series, using limit comparison when the terms are messy. Quote each test with its hypotheses.

notes.h: Absolute convergence, ratio and root tests, power series and exp
notes.body:
For series with terms of mixed sign, or complex terms, the key idea is absolute convergence. It leads to the ratio and root tests, and to power series, including the series definition of the exponential function.

Absolute and conditional convergence
- Σa_n converges absolutely if Σ|a_n| converges.
- Absolute convergence implies convergence, in both ℝ and ℂ. Proof: by the triangle inequality, |a_{n+1} + … + a_m| ≤ |a_{n+1}| + … + |a_m|, so the Cauchy criterion for Σ|a_n| gives it for Σa_n.
- A series that converges but not absolutely converges conditionally. Example: Σ(−1)^{n+1}/n.
- Rearrangements: any rearrangement of an absolutely convergent series converges to the same sum. Riemann's rearrangement theorem says a conditionally convergent real series can be rearranged to converge to any real number, or to diverge. The order of terms really matters.

Ratio test
- Suppose a_n ≠ 0 and |a_{n+1}/a_n| → L.
- If L < 1, Σa_n converges absolutely. If L > 1, Σa_n diverges (the terms do not tend to 0). If L = 1, the test is inconclusive.
- Both Σ1/n (divergent) and Σ1/n² (convergent) give L = 1.
- Example: Σ2ⁿ/n! has ratio 2/(n + 1) → 0, so it converges absolutely.

Root test
- If |a_n|^{1/n} → L, the same three conclusions hold. More generally, the root test can be stated with limsup |a_n|^{1/n} when the limit does not exist.
- The root test is at least as strong as the ratio test, but the ratio test is often easier to compute.

Power series
- A power series is Σc_n zⁿ, with z ∈ ℂ.
- Radius of convergence theorem: there is R ∈ [0, ∞] such that the series converges absolutely for |z| < R and diverges for |z| > R.
- Cauchy–Hadamard formula: 1/R = limsup |c_n|^{1/n}, with the conventions 1/0 = ∞ and 1/∞ = 0. When |c_{n+1}/c_n| has a limit L, R = 1/L.
- On the circle |z| = R anything can happen, and each point must be checked separately.

Examples
- Σzⁿ: R = 1, and it diverges at every point with |z| = 1 (the terms do not tend to 0).
- Σzⁿ/n: R = 1. At z = 1 it is the harmonic series, which diverges. At z = −1 it converges by the alternating series test.
- Σzⁿ/n²: R = 1, and it converges absolutely everywhere on |z| = 1.
- Σzⁿ/n!: R = ∞.
- Σn!zⁿ: R = 0, so it converges only at z = 0.

The exponential function
- exp(z) = Σ_{n=0}^∞ zⁿ/n! converges absolutely for every z ∈ ℂ.
- Multiplying absolutely convergent series (the Cauchy product) and using the binomial theorem gives exp(z + w) = exp(z)·exp(w).
- From this: exp(z) ≠ 0 and exp(−z) = 1/exp(z). Separately, one can show that e = exp(1) = lim(1 + 1/n)ⁿ.
- Defining cos and sin by their power series, Euler's formula exp(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ follows.

Exam tips: for a power series, find R first (ratio or root test on the coefficients), then test the boundary points one at a time with the nth-term, comparison or alternating series tests. Never claim the ratio test settles L = 1.

notes.h: Limits of functions, continuity, and the IVT and EVT
notes.body:
This topic moves from sequences to functions. The ε–δ definitions mirror the ε–N ones, and the sequential characterisation lets you reuse everything you know about sequences.

Limits of functions
- Let f be defined on a set D, and let a be a limit point of D. Then lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |f(x) − L| < ε for all x ∈ D with 0 < |x − a| < δ.
- The condition 0 < |x − a| means the value f(a), if it exists at all, is irrelevant to the limit.

Continuity
- f is continuous at a ∈ D if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |f(x) − f(a)| < ε for all x ∈ D with |x − a| < δ.
- f is continuous on D if it is continuous at every point of D.
- Sequential characterisation: f is continuous at a if and only if f(x_n) → f(a) for every sequence (x_n) in D with x_n → a.
- To show f is discontinuous at a, find one sequence x_n → a with f(x_n) not tending to f(a).
- Sums, products, quotients (where the denominator is non-zero) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous. So are polynomials, and power series inside their radius of convergence, including exp, sin and cos.

Examples
- f(x) = x sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0, with f(0) = 0, is continuous at 0, since |f(x)| ≤ |x|.
- sin(1/x) cannot be defined at 0 so as to be continuous: along x_n = 1/(nπ) the values are 0, but along x_n = 1/(2nπ + π/2) they are 1.
- The Dirichlet function (1 on ℚ, 0 off ℚ) is continuous nowhere, because rationals and irrationals are dense.
- ε–δ proof that x² is continuous at a: |x² − a²| = |x − a||x + a|. If |x − a| < 1, then |x + a| < 2|a| + 1. So take δ = min(1, ε/(2|a| + 1)).

Intermediate value theorem (IVT)
- Let f : [a, b] → ℝ be continuous. If y lies between f(a) and f(b), there is c ∈ [a, b] with f(c) = y.
- Proof idea: take c = sup{x ∈ [a, b] : f(x) < y} (for f(a) < y < f(b)) and use continuity to show f(c) = y. This relies on completeness.
- Example: p(x) = x⁵ − x − 1 has p(1) = −1 and p(2) = 29, so it has a root in (1, 2).
- Every real polynomial of odd degree has a real root.

Extreme value theorem (EVT)
- If f : [a, b] → ℝ is continuous on the closed, bounded interval [a, b], then f is bounded and attains its maximum and minimum values.
- Proof idea: use Bolzano–Weierstrass on a sequence of points whose values approach the supremum.
- Every hypothesis is needed. On (0, 1), f(x) = x has no maximum. On (0, 1], 1/x is unbounded. On [0, ∞), x is unbounded.

Uniform continuity
- f is uniformly continuous on D if δ can be chosen depending only on ε, not on the point.
- A continuous function on a closed, bounded interval is uniformly continuous. This is needed to prove that continuous functions are Riemann integrable.
- x² is continuous on ℝ but not uniformly continuous there.

Exam tips: state the IVT and EVT with all their hypotheses (continuous, closed and bounded interval), and in ε–δ proofs make δ explicit, using a preliminary bound such as |x − a| < 1 to control the other factors.

notes.h: Derivatives, Rolle's theorem, the MVT and Taylor's theorem
notes.body:
Differentiation is defined through a limit, and the main results (Rolle, the mean value theorem, Taylor's theorem) depend on the extreme value theorem, which in turn depends on completeness. Getting the hypotheses exactly right is where marks are won.

Definition
- Let f be defined on an open interval containing a. f is differentiable at a if lim_{h→0} (f(a + h) − f(a))/h exists. The limit is f′(a).
- Equivalently, f(a + h) = f(a) + f′(a)h + o(h): f is approximated by a straight line near a.
- Differentiable at a implies continuous at a, since f(a + h) − f(a) = h × (difference quotient) → 0 × f′(a) = 0.
- The converse is false: |x| is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there. The difference quotient is 1 from the right and −1 from the left.

Rules
- Sum, product and quotient rules (where the denominator is non-zero), and the chain rule, (g∘f)′(a) = g′(f(a))f′(a).
- Inverse functions: if f is continuous and strictly monotone on an open interval, differentiable at a and f′(a) ≠ 0, then (f⁻¹)′(f(a)) = 1/f′(a).
- Power series can be differentiated term by term inside their radius of convergence, which gives exp′ = exp.

Local extrema
- If f has a local maximum or minimum at an interior point c and f is differentiable at c, then f′(c) = 0.

Rolle's theorem
- Suppose f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b). Then there exists c ∈ (a, b) with f′(c) = 0.
- Proof: by the EVT, f attains a maximum and a minimum on [a, b]. If both occur at the endpoints, f is constant. Otherwise one occurs at an interior point, where f′ = 0.

Mean value theorem (MVT)
- Suppose f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b). Then there exists c ∈ (a, b) with f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).
- Proof: apply Rolle to g(x) = f(x) − f(a) − [(f(b) − f(a))/(b − a)](x − a).

Consequences of the MVT
- If f′ = 0 on an interval, f is constant there.
- If f′ > 0 on an interval, f is strictly increasing there.
- If |f′| ≤ K on an interval, then |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ K|x − y| there. For example, |sin x − sin y| ≤ |x − y|.

Cauchy MVT and L'Hôpital's rule
- Cauchy MVT: if f and g are continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), there is c ∈ (a, b) with (f(b) − f(a))g′(c) = (g(b) − g(a))f′(c).
- L'Hôpital (0/0 form): suppose f and g are differentiable on an open interval around a (except possibly at a), f(x), g(x) → 0 as x → a, and g′(x) ≠ 0 there. If f′(x)/g′(x) → L, then f(x)/g(x) → L.

Taylor's theorem (Lagrange remainder)
- If f⁽ⁿ⁾ is continuous on [a, x] and f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ exists on (a, x), then f(x) = Σ_{k=0}^{n} f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)(x − a)ᵏ/k! + f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)! for some ξ ∈ (a, x). (Similarly when x < a.)

A key example
- f(x) = x² sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0, with f(0) = 0, is differentiable everywhere, with f′(0) = 0.
- But f′(x) = 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x) for x ≠ 0 has no limit as x → 0.
- So a derivative need not be continuous.

Exam tips: before quoting Rolle or the MVT, check continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open one, and say so explicitly. To bound a difference |f(x) − f(y)|, think MVT.

notes.h: Riemann integration and the fundamental theorem of calculus
notes.body:
The integral is defined as a limiting construction: approximate the area from above and below using partitions, and ask whether the two approximations meet. This topic ties together completeness, uniform continuity and the mean value theorem.

Partitions and Darboux sums
- Let f be bounded on [a, b]. A partition is P = {a = x₀ < x₁ < … < x_n = b}.
- On each [x_{i−1}, x_i], let m_i = inf f and M_i = sup f there.
- The lower sum is L(f, P) = Σ m_i(x_i − x_{i−1}) and the upper sum is U(f, P) = Σ M_i(x_i − x_{i−1}).
- Refining a partition (adding points) cannot decrease L or increase U. For any partitions P and Q, L(f, P) ≤ U(f, Q).
- The lower integral is the supremum of all lower sums, and the upper integral the infimum of all upper sums. Completeness guarantees both exist.
- f is Riemann integrable when these two are equal, and the common value is ∫_a^b f.

Riemann's criterion
- A bounded f is integrable on [a, b] if and only if for every ε > 0 there is a partition P with U(f, P) − L(f, P) < ε.

Which functions are integrable?
- Monotone functions on [a, b]. With n equal subintervals, U − L = |f(b) − f(a)|(b − a)/n.
- Continuous functions on [a, b]. Uniform continuity makes M_i − m_i < ε/(b − a) on every subinterval of a fine enough partition.
- Bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities.
- Not integrable: the Dirichlet function on [0, 1] (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals). Every subinterval contains both kinds of number, so every lower sum is 0 and every upper sum is 1.

Worked example: f(x) = x on [0, 1], with P_n the partition into n equal parts.
- U = Σ (i/n)(1/n) = (n + 1)/(2n) and L = Σ ((i − 1)/n)(1/n) = (n − 1)/(2n).
- U − L = 1/n → 0, so f is integrable, and both sums tend to 1/2, so ∫_0^1 x dx = 1/2.

Properties
- The integral is linear: ∫(αf + βg) = α∫f + β∫g.
- It is monotone: if f ≤ g then ∫f ≤ ∫g.
- It is additive over intervals: ∫_a^b = ∫_a^c + ∫_c^b.
- |∫f| ≤ ∫|f|, and if |f| ≤ K then |∫_a^b f| ≤ K(b − a).
- If f is continuous, f ≥ 0 and ∫_a^b f = 0, then f ≡ 0 on [a, b].

Fundamental theorem of calculus
- Part 1: let f be integrable on [a, b] and F(x) = ∫_a^x f. Then F is continuous on [a, b] (indeed Lipschitz). If f is continuous at c ∈ (a, b), then F is differentiable at c and F′(c) = f(c).
- Part 2: if F is differentiable on [a, b] (one-sided derivatives at the endpoints) with F′ = f, and f is integrable on [a, b], then ∫_a^b f = F(b) − F(a). The proof applies the MVT on each subinterval of a partition.
- Combined with the chain rule: d/dx ∫_0^{g(x)} f(t) dt = f(g(x))g′(x) for continuous f and differentiable g. For example, d/dx ∫_0^{x²} cos t dt = 2x cos(x²).
- Integration by parts and substitution follow from the product rule and the chain rule.

Link back to series (integral test)
- If f is positive and decreasing on [1, ∞), then Σf(n) converges if and only if ∫_1^N f stays bounded as N → ∞. This gives another proof that Σ1/n^p converges exactly when p > 1.

Exam tips: when asked to show integrability from the definition, compute U(f, P_n) and L(f, P_n) for equal partitions and show that their difference tends to 0. When using either part of the FTC, state its hypotheses (integrable, continuous at the point, differentiable with integrable derivative).

questions.q: Let A = {1 − 1/n : n ∈ ℕ}, with ℕ = {1, 2, 3, …}. Which statement is correct?
options: sup A = 1, which is not attained, and inf A = 0, which is attained
max A = 1 and min A = 0
sup A does not exist because A has no largest element
sup A = 1 and inf A = 1/2
questions.why: Every element is below 1, and elements come arbitrarily close to 1, so sup A = 1. But 1 − 1/n = 1 has no solution, so 1 is not a maximum. The element at n = 1 is 0, the smallest, so inf A = min A = 0. Calling 1 the maximum mixes up supremum and maximum. Saying the supremum does not exist confuses it with the maximum; completeness guarantees a supremum here. inf A = 1/2 comes from starting at n = 2 instead of n = 1.

questions.q: Which of these is a correct statement of the completeness axiom for ℝ?
options: Every non-empty subset of ℝ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in ℝ
Every subset of ℝ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in ℝ
Every non-empty subset of ℝ has a least upper bound in ℝ
Every non-empty subset of ℚ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in ℚ
questions.why: The axiom needs both conditions: non-empty and bounded above. Dropping 'non-empty' fails for the empty set, which every real bounds above, so it has no least upper bound. Dropping 'bounded above' fails for ℕ. The version for ℚ is false, as {q ∈ ℚ : q² < 2} shows, and that failure is exactly what separates ℝ from ℚ.

questions.q: Let A = {1 − 1/n : n ∈ ℕ}. Prove that sup A = 1, stating where you use the Archimedean property.
markScheme: Shows 1 is an upper bound: 1 − 1/n < 1 for all n (1)
Uses the ε form: for any ε > 0 must find an element > 1 − ε (1)
Archimedean property gives n with 1/n < ε (1)
Then 1 − 1/n > 1 − ε, so no number below 1 is an upper bound; hence sup A = 1 (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Upper bound: for every n ∈ ℕ, 1/n > 0, so 1 − 1/n < 1. So 1 is an upper bound of A. Least: let ε > 0. By the Archimedean property there is n ∈ ℕ with n > 1/ε, that is, 1/n < ε. Then 1 − 1/n > 1 − ε, so 1 − ε is not an upper bound of A. Since this holds for every ε > 0, no number smaller than 1 is an upper bound, and so sup A = 1. (Note that 1 ∉ A, so the supremum is not attained.)

questions.q: To prove (2n + 1)/(n + 3) → 2 from the definition, you note that |a_n − 2| = 5/(n + 3). Given ε > 0, which choice of N works?
options: Any integer N > 5/ε
Any integer N > ε/5
Any integer N > 1/ε
No N works, because a_n never equals 2
questions.why: If n ≥ N > 5/ε then 5/(n + 3) < 5/n ≤ 5/N < ε, as required. N > ε/5 inverts the ratio: with ε = 0.1 it allows n = 1, where |a_1 − 2| = 1.25. N > 1/ε drops the factor 5: with ε = 0.1 and n = 11, |a_n − 2| = 5/14 ≈ 0.36, which is larger than ε. Convergence only needs the terms to get within ε of the limit, not to equal it.

questions.q: Which of these sequences converges?
options: √n
questions.why: |(−1)ⁿ/n| = 1/n → 0, so the sequence tends to 0. (−1)ⁿ is bounded but alternates between −1 and 1, so being bounded does not make it converge. √n is unbounded. It is tempting to think it converges because √(n + 1) − √n → 0, but consecutive differences tending to 0 do not make a sequence converge. (−1)ⁿ·n/(n + 1) has even-indexed terms tending to 1 and odd-indexed terms tending to −1, and two subsequences with different limits force divergence.

questions.q: (a) State what it means for a real sequence (a_n) to converge to a. (b) Prove from the definition that if a_n → a and b_n → b then a_n + b_n → a + b. (c) Prove that a convergent sequence is bounded.
markScheme: (a) Correct ε–N definition with quantifiers in the right order (1)
(b) Given ε, takes N₁, N₂ for ε/2 and N = max(N₁, N₂) (1)
(b) Triangle inequality: |a_n + b_n − a − b| ≤ |a_n − a| + |b_n − b| < ε (1)
(c) ε = 1 gives |a_n| ≤ |a| + 1 for n ≥ N (1)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) a_n → a means: for every ε > 0 there exists N ∈ ℕ such that |a_n − a| < ε for all n ≥ N. (b) Let ε > 0. Since a_n → a, there is N₁ with |a_n − a| < ε/2 for n ≥ N₁. Similarly there is N₂ with |b_n − b| < ε/2 for n ≥ N₂. Let N = max(N₁, N₂). For n ≥ N, the triangle inequality gives |(a_n + b_n) − (a + b)| ≤ |a_n − a| + |b_n − b| < ε/2 + ε/2 = ε. (c) Take ε = 1. There is N with |a_n − a| < 1 for n ≥ N, so |a_n| ≤ |a_n − a| + |a| < |a| + 1 for those n. Let M = max(|a_1|, …, |a_{N−1}|, |a| + 1). Then |a_n| ≤ M for every n, so (a_n) is bounded.

questions.q: Let a_1 = 1 and a_{n+1} = √(2 + a_n). What is lim a_n?
options: The sequence diverges because no term ever equals 2
questions.why: The sequence is increasing and bounded above by 2, so it converges. Its limit L satisfies L = √(2 + L), so L² − L − 2 = 0, giving L = 2 or L = −1. −1 is the other root of that quadratic, but every term is positive, so the limit cannot be negative. 1 is the first term, not the limit. A sequence need never reach its limit to converge to it.

questions.q: Which statement is the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem?
options: Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence
Every bounded sequence of real numbers converges
Every sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence
Every bounded sequence has a subsequence converging to the supremum of its terms
questions.why: The theorem guarantees only a convergent subsequence, and needs boundedness. 'Every bounded sequence converges' is false: (−1)ⁿ is bounded but diverges. Dropping boundedness fails for a_n = n, which has no convergent subsequence. Claiming the subsequence must converge to the supremum mixes the theorem up with monotone convergence: for a_n = (−1)ⁿ(1 + 1/n) the supremum of the terms is 3/2 (at n = 2), but every convergent subsequence tends to 1 or −1.

questions.q: Let a_1 = 1 and a_{n+1} = √(2 + a_n). Prove that (a_n) converges and find its limit, justifying each step.
markScheme: Induction: 0 < a_n < 2 for all n (1)
Induction or algebra: a_{n+1} > a_n, e.g. a_{n+1}² − a_n² = (2 − a_n)(1 + a_n) > 0 (1)
Monotone convergence theorem gives a_n → L (1)
Passing to the limit (continuity of √ or squaring): L² = 2 + L (1)
L ≥ 0 since a_n > 0, so L = 2, rejecting −1 (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Bounded: a_1 = 1 lies in (0, 2). If 0 < a_n < 2, then 2 < 2 + a_n < 4, so √2 < a_{n+1} < 2. By induction, 0 < a_n < 2 for all n. Increasing: a_{n+1}² − a_n² = 2 + a_n − a_n² = (2 − a_n)(1 + a_n) > 0, since 0 < a_n < 2. Both terms are positive, so a_{n+1} > a_n. By the monotone convergence theorem, (a_n) converges to some limit L. Squaring the recurrence gives a_{n+1}² = 2 + a_n. Letting n → ∞, and using the algebra of limits and the fact that (a_{n+1}) has the same limit as (a_n), gives L² = 2 + L, so L = 2 or L = −1. Since a_n > 0 for all n, L ≥ 0. Hence L = 2.

questions.q: Which of these series converges?
options: Σ 1/n²
Σ 1/n
Σ 1/√n
questions.why: Σ1/n² is a p-series with p = 2 > 1, so it converges. Σ1/n is the harmonic series: its terms tend to 0, but it still diverges, so a_n → 0 is not enough. Σ1/√n is a p-series with p = 1/2 ≤ 1, so it diverges (it is larger term by term than Σ1/n). Σn/(n + 1) has terms tending to 1, not 0, so it fails the nth-term test.

questions.q: What is Σ_{n=1}^∞ (2/3)ⁿ?
options: It diverges, because it has infinitely many positive terms
questions.why: Starting at n = 1, the sum is r/(1 − r) = (2/3)/(1/3) = 2. Using 1/(1 − r) = 3 counts an extra n = 0 term equal to 1. 0.6 is 1/(1 + r), which comes from a sign error in the geometric-series formula. A series with infinitely many positive terms can still converge if the partial sums are bounded, as they are here because |r| < 1.

questions.q: (a) Prove that Σ1/n diverges. (b) Prove that Σ1/n² converges. (c) Explain why (a) shows that the converse of the nth-term test is false.
markScheme: (a) So s_{2^k} ≥ 1 + k/2 → ∞; partial sums unbounded, so diverges (1)
(b) For n ≥ 2: 1/n² < 1/(n − 1) − 1/n, which telescopes (1)
(b) Partial sums bounded by 2 and increasing, so converge (monotone convergence) (1)
(c) 1/n → 0 yet Σ1/n diverges, so a_n → 0 does not imply convergence (1)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) For k ≥ 1, the block 1/(2^{k−1} + 1) + … + 1/2^k has 2^{k−1} terms, each at least 1/2^k, so the block is at least 1/2. Hence s_{2^k} ≥ 1 + k/2. The partial sums are unbounded, so Σ1/n diverges. (b) For n ≥ 2, 1/n² < 1/(n(n − 1)) = 1/(n − 1) − 1/n. Summing from n = 2 to N telescopes to 1 − 1/N < 1, so s_N < 2 for all N. The terms are positive, so (s_N) is increasing and bounded above, and it converges by the monotone convergence theorem. (c) The nth-term test says: if Σa_n converges then a_n → 0. Its converse would say: if a_n → 0 then Σa_n converges. The harmonic series has 1/n → 0 but diverges, so the converse is false.

questions.q: For the power series Σ_{n≥1} zⁿ/n, which statement is correct?
options: R = 1; it converges at z = −1 and diverges at z = 1
R = 1; it converges at every z with |z| = 1
R = ∞, because the coefficients 1/n tend to 0
R = 1; it diverges at every z with |z| = 1
questions.why: |c_{n+1}/c_n| = n/(n + 1) → 1, so R = 1. At z = 1 the series is harmonic and diverges, and at z = −1 it is alternating with decreasing terms tending to 0, so it converges. Claiming convergence on the whole circle ignores z = 1. Coefficients tending to 0 do not give R = ∞: R depends on how fast they tend to 0. Claiming divergence everywhere on the circle ignores z = −1.

questions.q: Suppose a_n ≠ 0 and |a_{n+1}/a_n| → 1. What can you conclude about Σa_n?
options: Nothing: the ratio test is inconclusive
It converges
It diverges
It converges conditionally but not absolutely
questions.why: When the limit ratio is exactly 1, the test gives no information. Σ1/n² (convergent) and Σ1/n (divergent) both have ratio limit 1, so neither 'converges' nor 'diverges' can be concluded. Conditional convergence is not forced either: Σ1/n² converges absolutely, and Σ1/n does not converge at all.

questions.q: Find the radius of convergence of Σ_{n≥1} n² zⁿ/3ⁿ, and determine for which z with |z| equal to that radius the series converges.
markScheme: On |z| = 3: |n²zⁿ/3ⁿ| = n² (1)
Terms do not tend to 0 (1)
So the series diverges at every point of |z| = 3 (1)
questions.modelAnswer: The coefficients are c_n = n²/3ⁿ. Then |c_{n+1}/c_n| = (n + 1)²/(3n²) = (1 + 1/n)²/3 → 1/3, so R = 3. (Equivalently, |c_n|^{1/n} = (n^{1/n})²/3 → 1/3.) The series converges absolutely for |z| < 3 and diverges for |z| > 3. On the circle |z| = 3, the terms have modulus n² × 3ⁿ/3ⁿ = n², which does not tend to 0. So the series fails the nth-term test, and diverges at every point with |z| = 3.

questions.q: Which of these functions on [0, 1] must take the value 0 somewhere in [0, 1]?
options: A continuous f with f(0) = −1 and f(1) = 2
f(x) = −1 for x < 1/2 and f(x) = 2 for x ≥ 1/2
A continuous f with f(0) = 1 and f(1) = 2
An f with f(0) = −1 and f(1) = 2 that is differentiable on (0, 1)
questions.why: The IVT applies to a function continuous on [0, 1], and 0 lies between −1 and 2. The step function has the same end values but jumps over 0, so it is not continuous. The continuous function with f(0) = 1 and f(1) = 2 has no sign change, so the IVT says nothing: f(x) = 1 + x never vanishes. Being differentiable on the open interval does not make f continuous at the endpoints: f(0) = −1 with f(x) = 1 + x for 0 < x ≤ 1 is differentiable on (0, 1) and never zero.

questions.q: Which function is guaranteed to attain a maximum value on the given set?
options: f(x) = x² on [−1, 2]
questions.why: x² is continuous on the closed, bounded interval [−1, 2], so by the extreme value theorem it attains a maximum (4, at x = 2). On (0, 1), x has supremum 1 but never reaches it, because the interval is open. On (0, 1], 1/x is unbounded near 0, so the interval failing to be closed at 0 lets the function blow up. On [0, ∞), x is unbounded, because the interval is not bounded.

questions.q: (a) Prove that the equation x⁵ − x − 1 = 0 has a real solution in (1, 2). (b) Prove from the ε–δ definition that f(x) = x² is continuous at every a ∈ ℝ.
markScheme: (a) p is a polynomial, hence continuous on [1, 2] (1)
(a) p(1) = −1 < 0 < 29 = p(2); IVT gives c with p(c) = 0, and c ≠ 1, 2 so c ∈ (1, 2) (1)
(b) δ = min(1, ε/(2|a| + 1)) gives |x² − a²| < ε (1)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) p(x) = x⁵ − x − 1 is a polynomial, so it is continuous on [1, 2]. p(1) = 1 − 1 − 1 = −1 and p(2) = 32 − 2 − 1 = 29. Since 0 lies between −1 and 29, the IVT gives c ∈ [1, 2] with p(c) = 0, and c ≠ 1, 2 because p(1), p(2) ≠ 0, so c ∈ (1, 2). (b) Let a ∈ ℝ and ε > 0. Put δ = min(1, ε/(2|a| + 1)) > 0. If |x − a| < δ then |x − a| < 1, so |x + a| ≤ |x − a| + 2|a| < 2|a| + 1. Hence |x² − a²| = |x − a||x + a| < (ε/(2|a| + 1)) × (2|a| + 1) = ε. So f is continuous at a.

questions.q: f(x) = |x| on [−1, 1] satisfies f(−1) = f(1), but there is no c ∈ (−1, 1) with f′(c) = 0. Which hypothesis of Rolle's theorem fails?
options: f is not differentiable at 0
f is not continuous on [−1, 1]
f is not increasing on [−1, 1]
questions.why: |x| has a corner at 0: the difference quotient is −1 from the left and 1 from the right, so f is not differentiable on all of (−1, 1). It is continuous on [−1, 1], so continuity does not fail. f(−1) = f(1) = 1, so the endpoint condition holds. Rolle's theorem has no monotonicity hypothesis, and a function satisfying its conditions typically is not monotone.

questions.q: f is differentiable on ℝ with |f′(x)| ≤ 3 for all x, and f(0) = 1. What is the largest possible value of f(2)?
questions.why: By the MVT, f(2) − f(0) = 2f′(c) for some c, so f(2) ≤ 1 + 2 × 3 = 7, and f(x) = 1 + 3x shows 7 is attained. 6 is the largest possible increase, 2 × 3, which forgets to add f(0) = 1. 4 = 1 + 3 forgets to multiply by the interval length 2. 1 would follow only if f′ were 0; a bound on |f′| does not make f constant.

questions.q: (a) State the mean value theorem. (b) Use it to prove that |sin x − sin y| ≤ |x − y| for all real x, y. (c) Prove that if f is differentiable on an interval I with f′(x) = 0 for all x ∈ I, then f is constant on I.
markScheme: (a) Correct statement with continuity on [a, b] and differentiability on (a, b) (1)
(b) sin is differentiable everywhere; MVT on [y, x] gives sin x − sin y = cos(c)(x − y) (1)
(b) |cos c| ≤ 1 gives the inequality; the case x = y is trivial (1)
(c) For x < y in I, MVT on [x, y] (valid since differentiable implies continuous) gives f(y) − f(x) = f′(c)(y − x) (1)
(c) f′(c) = 0, so f(x) = f(y) for all x, y, so f is constant (1)
questions.modelAnswer: (a) If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then there exists c ∈ (a, b) with f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). (b) If x = y there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, assume y < x. sin is differentiable on ℝ, so the MVT on [y, x] gives c ∈ (y, x) with sin x − sin y = cos(c)(x − y). Since |cos c| ≤ 1, |sin x − sin y| ≤ |x − y|. (c) Take any x < y in I. f is differentiable on I, hence continuous on [x, y] and differentiable on (x, y). The MVT gives c ∈ (x, y) with f(y) − f(x) = f′(c)(y − x) = 0. So f takes the same value at every pair of points, and f is constant on I.

questions.q: Let f(x) = 1 if x is rational and f(x) = 0 if x is irrational, on [0, 1]. Which statement is correct for the Riemann integral?
options: f is not Riemann integrable: every lower sum is 0 and every upper sum is 1
f is integrable with integral 0, because the rationals are countable
f is integrable with integral 1, because the rationals are dense
f is integrable with integral 1/2, the average of the upper and lower sums
questions.why: Every subinterval of any partition contains both rationals and irrationals, so m_i = 0 and M_i = 1 throughout, giving L = 0 and U = 1 for every partition. The lower and upper integrals differ, so f is not Riemann integrable. 'Integral 0 because the rationals are countable' is the Lebesgue answer, which is a different theory. Density of the rationals gives sup f = 1 on each piece, but that only fixes the upper sum. Averaging U and L is not part of the definition: integrability needs them to meet.

questions.q: Let F(x) = ∫_0^{x²} cos t dt. What is F′(x)?
options: 2x cos(x²)
cos(x²)
sin(x²)
2x cos x
questions.why: Write F = G∘g, with G(u) = ∫_0^u cos t dt and g(x) = x². By FTC part 1, G′(u) = cos u, so the chain rule gives F′(x) = cos(x²) × 2x. cos(x²) forgets the chain-rule factor g′(x) = 2x. sin(x²) is F(x) itself, not its derivative. 2x cos x substitutes x instead of x² into the integrand.

questions.q: Using equal partitions P_n of [0, 1] into n subintervals, show from the definition that f(x) = x is Riemann integrable on [0, 1] and that ∫_0^1 x dx = 1/2. You may use Σ_{i=1}^n i = n(n + 1)/2.
markScheme: f increasing, so on [(i−1)/n, i/n]: m_i = (i − 1)/n, M_i = i/n (1)
U − L = 1/n → 0, so by Riemann's criterion f is integrable (1)
L(f, P_n) ≤ ∫f ≤ U(f, P_n) and both tend to 1/2, so ∫ = 1/2 (1)
questions.modelAnswer: f is increasing, so on [(i − 1)/n, i/n] its infimum is (i − 1)/n and its supremum is i/n. Then U(f, P_n) = Σ_{i=1}^n (i/n)(1/n) = (1/n²) × n(n + 1)/2 = (n + 1)/(2n), and L(f, P_n) = Σ_{i=1}^n ((i − 1)/n)(1/n) = (1/n²) × (n − 1)n/2 = (n − 1)/(2n). So U − L = 1/n. Given ε > 0, choose n > 1/ε; then U − L < ε, and f is integrable by Riemann's criterion. The integral lies between L(f, P_n) and U(f, P_n) for every n. Both tend to 1/2, so ∫_0^1 x dx = 1/2.

questions.q:
(a) Define what it means for a sequence (a_n) of real numbers to be a Cauchy sequence. [2]
(b) Prove that every convergent real sequence is Cauchy. [3]
(c) State the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem. Prove that every Cauchy sequence of real numbers is bounded, and hence that it converges. [7]
(d) Determine whether Σ_{n≥1} (−1)ⁿ/√n converges absolutely, converges conditionally, or diverges. Justify your answer. [4]
(e) Use the ratio test to show that Σ_{n≥1} n!/nⁿ converges. [4]
markScheme: (b) N for ε/2; |a_m − a_n| ≤ |a_m − a| + |a − a_n| < ε (3)
(c) B–W: every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence (1)
(c) Cauchy ⇒ bounded with ε = 1: |a_n| ≤ max(|a_1|, …, |a_{N−1}|, |a_N| + 1) (2)
(c) Subsequence a_{n_k} → a; for ε, combine Cauchy N and subsequence K, then |a_n − a| ≤ |a_n − a_{n_k}| + |a_{n_k} − a| < ε (4)
(d) 1/√n decreasing to 0, so the alternating series test gives convergence; Σ1/√n is a p-series with p = 1/2 ≤ 1, so it diverges; conditionally convergent (4)
(e) a_{n+1}/a_n = (n/(n + 1))ⁿ = 1/(1 + 1/n)ⁿ → 1/e < 1, so it converges (4)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) (a_n) is Cauchy if for every ε > 0 there exists N ∈ ℕ such that |a_m − a_n| < ε for all m, n ≥ N.

(b) Suppose a_n → a and let ε > 0. Choose N with |a_n − a| < ε/2 for all n ≥ N. Then for m, n ≥ N: |a_m − a_n| ≤ |a_m − a| + |a − a_n| < ε/2 + ε/2 = ε. So (a_n) is Cauchy.

(c) Bolzano–Weierstrass: every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence.
Bounded: let (a_n) be Cauchy. With ε = 1 there is N such that |a_m − a_n| < 1 for all m, n ≥ N. In particular |a_n| < |a_N| + 1 for n ≥ N. So |a_n| ≤ M := max(|a_1|, …, |a_{N−1}|, |a_N| + 1) for every n.
Convergent: by Bolzano–Weierstrass, some subsequence (a_{n_k}) converges, say to a. Let ε > 0. Choose N with |a_m − a_n| < ε/2 for all m, n ≥ N, and choose K with |a_{n_k} − a| < ε/2 for all k ≥ K. Take any n ≥ N, and pick k ≥ K with n_k ≥ N, which is possible because n_k → ∞. Then |a_n − a| ≤ |a_n − a_{n_k}| + |a_{n_k} − a| < ε/2 + ε/2 = ε. Hence a_n → a. This uses completeness through Bolzano–Weierstrass, and the result fails in ℚ.

(d) Let b_n = 1/√n. Then b_n > 0, (b_n) is decreasing and b_n → 0, so by the alternating series test Σ(−1)ⁿ b_n converges. However, Σ|(−1)ⁿ/√n| = Σ1/√n is a p-series with p = 1/2 ≤ 1, so it diverges (it is larger term by term than the harmonic series). So the series converges conditionally, not absolutely.

(e) Let a_n = n!/nⁿ > 0. Then a_{n+1}/a_n = [(n + 1)!/(n + 1)^{n+1}] × [nⁿ/n!] = (n + 1)nⁿ/(n + 1)^{n+1} = (n/(n + 1))ⁿ = 1/(1 + 1/n)ⁿ. Since (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e, the ratio tends to 1/e < 1. By the ratio test, Σn!/nⁿ converges (absolutely).

questions.q:
(a) Define what it means for f : ℝ → ℝ to be (i) continuous at a and (ii) differentiable at a. [3]
(b) Prove that if f is differentiable at a then f is continuous at a. Give an example showing that the converse is false, with justification. [4]
(c) Let f(x) = x² sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = 0. Show that f is differentiable at every point of ℝ, find f′(x), and show that f′ is not continuous at 0. [7]
(d) Let g : [a, b] → ℝ be continuous with g(x) ≥ 0 for all x and ∫_a^b g = 0 (where a < b). Prove that g(x) = 0 for all x ∈ [a, b]. [6]
markScheme: (a) ε–δ continuity; limit of difference quotient for differentiability (3)
(b) f(a + h) − f(a) = h × [difference quotient] → 0 × f′(a) = 0 (2)
(b) |x| at 0: difference quotient is ±1 from the two sides, so no limit; but |x| is continuous (2)
(c) For x ≠ 0: product and chain rules give f′(x) = 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x) (2)
(c) x_n = 1/(2nπ) → 0 gives f′(x_n) = −1, which does not tend to f′(0) = 0, so f′ is discontinuous at 0 (3)
(d) Suppose g(c) > 0; continuity gives δ with g > g(c)/2 on an interval J ⊆ [a, b] of positive length ℓ (3)
(d) ∫_a^b g ≥ ∫_J g ≥ (g(c)/2)ℓ > 0 using g ≥ 0 elsewhere; contradiction (3)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a)(i) f is continuous at a if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |x − a| < δ implies |f(x) − f(a)| < ε.
(ii) f is differentiable at a if lim_{h→0} (f(a + h) − f(a))/h exists (as a real number). Its value is f′(a).

(b) For h ≠ 0, f(a + h) − f(a) = h × [(f(a + h) − f(a))/h]. As h → 0, the first factor tends to 0 and the second to f′(a), so by the algebra of limits the product tends to 0 × f′(a) = 0. Hence f(a + h) → f(a), and f is continuous at a.
For the converse, take f(x) = |x| at a = 0. It is continuous, since ||x| − 0| = |x| < ε whenever |x| < δ = ε. But (|h| − 0)/h equals 1 for h > 0 and −1 for h < 0, so the limit as h → 0 does not exist, and f is not differentiable at 0.

(c) At 0: (f(h) − f(0))/h = h sin(1/h), and |h sin(1/h)| ≤ |h| → 0, so f′(0) = 0 by the sandwich theorem.
For x ≠ 0, f is a product and composition of differentiable functions near x, so f′(x) = 2x sin(1/x) + x² cos(1/x) × (−1/x²) = 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x). So f is differentiable everywhere.
To show f′ is not continuous at 0, let x_n = 1/(2nπ) → 0. Then sin(1/x_n) = 0 and cos(1/x_n) = 1, so f′(x_n) = −1 for every n. This does not tend to f′(0) = 0, so by the sequential characterisation f′ is not continuous at 0. (In fact lim_{x→0} f′(x) does not exist: 2x sin(1/x) → 0, while cos(1/x) oscillates.)

(d) Suppose, for a contradiction, that g(c) > 0 for some c ∈ [a, b]. By continuity, with ε = g(c)/2, there is δ > 0 such that g(x) > g(c)/2 for all x ∈ [a, b] with |x − c| < δ. The set J = [a, b] ∩ [c − δ/2, c + δ/2] is a closed interval of positive length ℓ > 0, since a < b. (If c is an endpoint, J extends to one side only.) Because g ≥ 0 on [a, b], monotonicity and additivity of the integral give ∫_a^b g ≥ ∫_J g ≥ (g(c)/2) × ℓ > 0. This contradicts ∫_a^b g = 0. So g(x) = 0 for every x ∈ [a, b]. Continuity is essential: a function that is 0 except for the value 1 at a single point is non-negative and has integral 0, but is not identically zero.
